message.content:
The sea appears most often as **a deep blue**—the same hue you see when looking at clear water on a sunny day. That classic “azure” look comes from how sunlight interacts with seawater:

| Factor | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| **Water absorption** | Water absorbs longer‑wavelength light (red, orange) more strongly than shorter wavelengths (blue), so what’s left after scattering looks bluish. |
| **Depth & clarity** | Shallow or sandy bottoms reflect green/amber tones; deeper waters absorb everything but leave a richer navy or indigo shade. |
| **Angle of view** | Looking up through air gives a lighter sky‑blued tone; viewing directly down into the ocean can reveal darker blues or even greens if phytoplankton are present. |
| **Sun position** | Early morning or late afternoon sunsets give the surface a golden or pink glow; midday sun produces crisp, bright azure. |

So while we usually think of the sea as blue, its true palette ranges across blues, turquoise, teal, and sometimes green or gray depending on conditions.
